data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because any rational basis for preferring one theory over another for future action inherently assumes the uniformity of nature or the reliability of past performance as a guide to the future.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one can formulate a notion of 'rational preference' that is entirely disconnected from expectations of future success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice is framed purely as a methodological rule for generating new tests rather than a guide for practical action.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'bet' is acknowledged as a blind guess, rendering the preference irrational but psychologically inevitable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Even if Popper labels the preference 'pragmatic,' the moment a scientist chooses Theory A over Theory B for practical application (e.g., building a bridge), they are effectively betting that Theory A will continue to hold. This bet is an inductive leap: it assumes that the structural features that allowed A to survive past tests will persist in future, untested instances. Without this assumption, the choice is arbitrary. Therefore, the 'preference' is functionally identical to assigning a higher subjective probability, violating Popper's core prohibition against induction.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
